1:
Every commentator begins by noticing that the chapter stands out of its place. Clarke is the most exasperated, asking what strange confusion has put these chapters in this order, and who could have expected to hear of Jehoiakim again. Gill measures the gap at seventeen years, since the preceding prophecies belong to the tenth and eleventh years of Zedekiah; Ellicott agrees on about seventeen, adding that Jerusalem was not yet besieged. Wesley makes it ten or eleven years, and Calvin fifteen before the destruction of the city.

Calvin turns the discrepancy into an account of how the book came to exist. The prophets, he says, reduced their preaching afterwards to a summary; a copy was affixed to the doors of the temple, and the books now extant were formed from these. Jeremiah, he concludes, did not write the book, but his discourses were collected into a volume without regard to the order of time.

On who the Rechabites were the answers converge and then part. Gill and Wesley identify them with the Kenites, descended from Hobab, also called Jethro. Henry stresses the distinctness: they kept by themselves and were no more numbered with the families of Israel than with the nations. Clarke fills in the manner of life, describing them as herdsmen feeding their flocks in the deserts, who considered the life of cities the death of liberty, believing they would dishonour themselves by using food that obliged them to live a sedentary life. Their whole property being cattle and tents was easily removable, and their way of living was not likely to excite envy in those who had learned to relish the luxuries of life. Keil and Delitzsch add the occasion, that this family had fled for refuge to Jerusalem before the approach of the Chaldeans.

Ellicott presses further into the founder and offers the most speculative reading in the chapter. Jonadab appears in the history as the ally of Jehu in the overthrow of the house of Ahab. But since the word for Rechab means chariot, and the same word was applied to Elijah, Ellicott thinks it likely that son of Rechab means son of the chariot, that is, disciple of the great prophet. He reads the whole discipline as a threefold protest, against the worship that had flowed into Israel from Phoenicia, against the corruption of the life of cities, and against the intemperance that was tainting the nation, and compares it to the ascetic sects that have arisen in Arabia. Henry dates Jonadab to the days of Jehu, nearly three hundred years before this, and recalls that the rising prince courted him when he wished to appear zealous, thinking nothing more likely to confirm the people in that opinion than to have so good a man ride in the chariot with him. Clarke puts the interval at upwards of two hundred and fifty years.

Calvin alone asks why the wine was to be set before them in the temple rather than in a private house. The priests were forbidden wine only while serving, and the Levites who kept watch were allowed it in those very chambers; so if wine could be drunk by the ministers themselves, what excuse remained for the people when men of the common sort refused it on nothing but their father command? Had God forbidden the whole nation the use of wine the law might have seemed too rigid. Calvin adds that the security of the kingdom under Jehoiakim kept them from attending to spoken words, so a visible sign was necessary to make them ashamed. Keil and Delitzsch supply the setting: Jaazaniah was probably the chief of the family then, and the chamber of the sons of Hanan stood next the chamber of the princes. They also settle a point of construction, that the honourable title man of God belongs to Hanan rather than to Jigdaliah his father.
3:
Ellicott reads the list of names as evidence rather than genealogy. Jaazaniah means that Jehovah hears, Jeremiah that Jehovah exalts, Habaziniah that Jehovah gathers, and such names show that the Rechabites shared the faith of Israel; he adds that the recurrence of the prophet own name may point to some earlier connexion between the two families. If they were a religious order rather than a household, then the brethren and the sons may mark degrees of membership, the brethren fully incorporated and the sons still probationers in training, as the sons of the prophets were. Gill and Clarke keep to the plainer reading, that Jaazaniah was the leading man of the family and that the whole house means the family.

Calvin asks why the scene was staged where it was, and answers from publicity. A thing done in an obscure corner may be thought doubtful or fabulous, so the prophet chose a well-known place, that the report might spread through the whole city and that the dignity of the place might add credit to it. The place, he says, was select, so that it might serve as a notable theatre and the prophecy gain more credit. He also notes in passing that the word for vessel stands here by a change of number for all the sacred furniture of the temple.

Ellicott fills in the architecture. The temple had apartments built in its precincts, like a cathedral, assigned by special favour as residences for conspicuous priests or prophets; Huldah seems to have lived in such a set of rooms, known as the college. This chamber belonged to the sons of Hanan, and Jeremiah appears from the narrative to have had no chamber of his own. Ellicott takes the sons of Hanan for a company of scholars under that prophet training, so that Jeremiah is introducing the two religious orders to each other. The princes were official persons entitled to residence, and the keeper of the door probably belonged to the higher section of the priesthood; and the stress laid on all these details was meant to show that the scene was acted in the presence of representatives of the priestly, the prophetic and the official orders.

On whom the title man of God belongs to there is a disagreement. Clarke and Wesley attach it to Igdaliah, taking him for a prophet or holy man with some office in the temple, while Ellicott holds the Hebrew punctuation decisive in favour of Hanan. Gill accounts for the wine itself, supposing the prophet drew the vessels from the chambers where such things were kept, and that the company gathered was large enough to need pots as well as cups. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two, the larger being bowls out of which the drinking cups were filled.

Calvin counts the injunctions and then asks the harder question. Four things were laid on them, to drink no wine, to cultivate no fields, to plant no vineyards, and to build no houses; and to these a promise of long life was joined for those who obeyed. But was the father right to forbid it? Agriculture, Calvin says, is in itself a mode of living not only honest and innocent but remote from ambition, fraud and plunder, and seems of all kinds the simplest; on that ground the advice might well be blamed. His answer is circumstantial rather than principled. Seeing the people despise the law of their God, Jonadab looked for a vengeance which did not follow for a long time but ought even then to have been dreaded; and seeing the sources of the vices around him, he wished his posterity accustomed to an austere manner of living, so that they might move more easily and endure with quieter minds whatever adversity came, being neither rich nor settled enough to have much to lose.
6:
Clarke reduces the whole discipline to three precepts and gives each a spiritual reading. To drink no wine is to preserve the body in temperance, lest a man do what is prejudicial to himself, injurious to his neighbour or dishonourable to his God. To build no house is to become resident nowhere and not to court earthly possessions, living free from ambition and envy and therefore free from contention and strife. To dwell in tents is to imitate Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the rest of the patriarchs, who were strangers and pilgrims looking for a better country. He grants that there must necessarily be more in the injunctions than meets the eye in the account. Wesley adds that the tents were moveable habitations that could be shifted with little labour to feed the flocks.

Calvin asks why the account is drawn out at such length, and answers that the object is to amplify their constancy. A man may obey his father and yet not be so fixed in purpose that he might not fail on some slight occasion; here the wine stood before them and they refused it as though no temptation had been offered, though the man who commanded them had been dead for ages. The Nazarites were forbidden wine, but only until their vow was performed, and the priest while discharging his duty; both afterwards resumed their ordinary way of living, whereas to taste no wine throughout a whole life is far harder. Nor was it a single point of obedience, since the same father bound them to a wandering life and to possess nothing.

On the house both Gill and Calvin notice that the prohibition falls on dwelling and not on building. They might assist in raising splendid palaces and gain a livelihood by that labour, and were forbidden only to inhabit them. Wesley and Gill both put the interval at three hundred years or thereabouts.

The presence of the family inside the walls needs explaining. Clarke has them plead necessity, that if they appear to be acting contrary to their institutions in being found in a city, nothing but the preservation of their lives has induced them to take the step. Ellicott calls the statement an apologetic explanation, and reads it as a temporary casualty: they had been driven in like the peasants of Judea, and meant to return to their old manner of life when the danger was past. Keil and Delitzsch note that it was the arrival of Nebuchadnezzar that brought them, and raise a question about the second army named beside the Chaldeans, suggesting that the Syrians are mentioned because of predatory incursions on Israel and Judah at an earlier period.

Calvin turns the refuge into an argument for the discipline itself, that it had proved advantageous to them. Had they been fixed to their possessions they must have gone into exile with the rest, and what happened to the ten tribes would have happened to them; but owning nothing they were freer to move, and were spared the trial of leaving anything behind. Many, he says, are so tied to their houses and fields and vineyards and meadows that they would rather be killed a hundred times than be torn away from them; these could gather in a single day all that they had. Their poverty was a great advantage and their austerity a benefit, for they could live in the city without difficulty, needing no luxuries; whereas men accustomed to wine and delicacies might have debated whether it were not better to die at once than to suffer want in a besieged town. That, Calvin concludes, is what the father had in view: foreseeing what revolutions were at hand, he trained his posterity so that when the difficulty came they would not sink under it, but bear want patiently where others would find it intolerable.
12:
Ellicott marks the transition. Until now the prophet had acted on a thought that came to him as an inspiration, with only a partial insight into its meaning; at these words he passes at once into the prophetic state. He infers from the blessing at the end of the chapter that the speech was uttered in the hearing of the Rechabites, forming the conclusion of the strange dramatic scene.

Henry sets out the comparison as a series of aggravations. The Rechabites obeyed one who was but a man like themselves, the father of their flesh, while this people disobeyed an eternal God who had absolute authority over them as the Father of their spirits. Jonadab was long since dead and ignorant of them, able neither to take notice of disobedience nor to punish it, whereas God lives for ever and stands ready to avenge. And the Rechabites were never once reminded of their obligation, while this people had prophets sent again and again to put them in mind of their duty. He puts the opening question with the same force: will you not at length receive instruction, will nothing affect you, will nothing fasten upon you? Gill makes the contrast from the titles, the speaker being the Lord of armies in heaven and earth and the Creator of Israel, infinitely greater than the man whose precepts his posterity had kept.

Calvin notices that the reproof is put into the mouth of God himself, to make it more effectual. On the word rendered instruction he observes that it can mean ruling or governing as well as correction, and takes the complaint to be against a hardness long persisted in, as though God asked whether this people would always be so ungovernably wanton as never to submit to the yoke. But nothing unjust was required, so that no excuse of rigour could be pretended. I require only that you obey me, he has God say, and this is all my severity; I demand nothing but what children ought to render their fathers willingly and without being admonished.

Gill observes that wine is agreeable to the nature of man and cheers the heart, and was never prohibited these men by any law of God; they abstained because their father had forbidden it. Calvin draws the contrast into a principle: the precept was hard, and there was no scruple of conscience to keep them from wine, only the authority of a man who was dead, and yet it prevailed; whereas God asked nothing but that his people receive his law and not go astray after alien gods. Ellicott makes the same argument formally, since words kept as a rule of life for three hundred years by a family are set against words neglected by a people adopted as children, who had besides the same promise that obedience would keep them in the land, and turned a deaf ear to it. He notes that rising early and speaking is a phrase characteristic of this prophet.

Calvin ends on the difference in method. Jonadab gave his command once only, and that command, which might easily have been forgotten, remained perpetually in the hearts of his sons, so that they taught it to their grandsons; God commanded what was right not once but rising early, which Calvin takes as a metaphor for anticipating them, not waiting until a long licence had made them more addicted to their vices. Men who have gone many years without restraint, he says, become habitually refractory; and from this he draws the rule that those who are to be ruled by us must be formed from infancy, since a wantonness allowed to run cannot afterwards be restrained by any laws. Clarke reads the episode as a deliberate test, the Lord knowing the fidelity of this family and trying them so that their obedience might show the people their own ingratitude.
15:
The sending of the prophets is treated by all four as the weight that tips the comparison. Gill notes that they were sent one after another ever since the times of Moses to explain and enforce the laws, a circumstance with no parallel on the other side, since the Rechabites kept their father charge without reminders. Calvin makes the same point as an anticipation of excuses. Had Moses alone commanded what was right, the people might have pretended that the law was buried and forgotten; so God sent many, and so many that the doctrine was continually proclaimed in their hearing. And he draws the conclusion: men otherwise tardy and even refractory grow gentle when recalled to their duty every day and hour, so that when this people still refused, their madness became the more evident. Ellicott adds a point of dating, that the summons to return from an evil way is not a general summary of earlier preaching but an almost verbal reproduction of what this prophet had preached in the fourth year of the reign, before the incident here recorded.

Calvin then presses the ease of what was asked. Had no law been written at all, natural light would have been enough to teach them that it was their duty to obey, since the law of obedience is written on our hearts as a testimony and no one can justly plead ignorance. He required nothing but what nature itself dictated, that they should repent and form their life by the rule of obedience; and though no prophet had been among them, every man ought to have been his own teacher. Set beside the hard precept about wine, that is the difference the chapter is built on.

Calvin explains why the contrast is made twice. The indignity appears more fully when the two sides are set out again: on the one hand a mortal man, now dead, retained authority over his posterity though he had laid on them a restraint hard and difficult; on the other God effected nothing, although he had constantly exhorted his people, had sent prophets and never ceased to invite them, and had not only invited but kindly allured them by setting his favours before them and giving them hope for the time to come. Since every means had been tried without success, the hopeless depravity of the people stood revealed. Gill says the design of the contrast is to aggravate and expose the sin.

Clarke marks the turn to sentence: having clearly convicted them of ingratitude and rebellion by the conduct of this family, the prophet proceeds to pronounce judgment. Calvin thinks the order deliberate: the final sentence, which he calls a thunderbolt, is not brought forward until the guilt has been proved. Ellicott hears in the complaint a reproduction of the prophet own earlier words, and observes that it has been the ever recurring burden of all teachers of wisdom and of all true prophets.

The last observation turns on two prepositions barely distinguishable from one another. God had spoken to them, Calvin says, and now he speaks against them; the one word covers doctrine, exhortation and whatever may lead a man to repentance, while the other covers threatening, to which God has recourse only after finding that teaching does nothing. What he draws from it is that when men reject the word of teaching they do not escape speech altogether, but fall under the other word, which denounces judgment. Teaching looks useless when it is not received, but whoever despises it will find at last, to his own ruin, that the denunciations ratifying the authority of that word are not empty. Calvin adds that the speaking against them is not to be understood of words only, since God would now command the Chaldeans, who were to be his ministers and the executioners of his vengeance.
18:
Ellicott is careful to say what the blessing does not establish. The words decide nothing about whether the commandment binds anyone else; the law this prophet received laid down no such rule, and a righteous life was possible without it. What he was taught to praise was the loyalty with which these men adhered to a merely human precept, not at variance with the letter of any divine law and designed, like the Nazarite vow, to carry the spirit of that law to its highest point. He then generalises: a temper of faithfulness to any rule of life sanctioned by prescription, whether it be that of a school, a college, a guild or a religious order, is in itself praiseworthy compared with individual self-assertion and self-will.

Calvin sets the reward on the commandment about parents, the first to which a promise is annexed, that a man honour his father and his mother and so prolong his life; it is no wonder a reward followed. But he draws the limit sharply. Had they followed their father in an unlawful thing they would have deserved punishment, and their obedience was approved only because this precept was not inconsistent with the law of God; where laws are framed to set up modes of worship of human invention they are impious, and to lay necessity on consciences is a tyrannical bondage. That was not the character of what Jonadab enjoined. It was useful, referred only to things of this life, and did not bind the conscience: when necessity came they moved to Jerusalem and lived as others in houses, not pitching tents inside the walls but taking hired dwellings, and were still held to have kept their father command.

On the promise itself Ellicott collects a long history of afterlives. In an early account of the death of James the Just, Hegesippus names the sons of the Rechabites looking on in reverential sympathy with a man whose life, like theirs, carried the Nazarite type to its highest perfection. Benjamin of Tudela in the twelfth century reported finding a hundred thousand Jews called Rechabites governed by a prince of the house of David, and travellers met tribes near Mecca who kept the rule, claimed the descent and cited this verse as fulfilled in them. Ellicott is cautious about the recent cases, thinking they show the effect of the later ascetic movement among the Arabs, which identified its own rule with the old practice.

The one open dispute is over the phrase about standing before God. Ellicott points out that it carries a distinct secondary sense in Hebrew, a liturgical expression for the ministrations of the Levites who were chosen to stand before the Lord. Calvin rejects that reading by name, noting that some of the Rabbins applied the passage to the priesthood on exactly this ground, since it is often said of the Levites and the priests that they stood before the face of God, and calling the inference strained. His plain sense is that God simply intimates that some of the offspring would always be living, and that by his special favour, so that their obedience might not appear to be without its just reward.

Clarke takes the promise as one of honour and continuance: the name shall be honourable, the posterity shall have continual protection, and there shall never be a time in which men of that spirit are wanting as patterns of genuine simplicity, filial obedience, purity of manners and deadness to the world. He passes on the suggestion that a later ascetic order were literally their descendants, in which case the promise is fulfilled to the letter. Wesley cuts the term down, taking the for ever here to mean the duration of that state and church. Gill grounds the whole on the same commandment, that God has enjoined obedience to parents and has promised to reward it.
